Longitudinal Mixed-Model Calibration Simulation (Goal 5a)

mlmRev::egsingle two-stage hierarchical plasmode resampling

2026-11-18

1 Purpose

This report documents Goal 5a of the RESI mixed-model extension project (see instructions/instructions.md at the repository root): a calibration check of the mixed-model RESI point estimator and of the fixed-effect standard errors for lme4::lmer, using a hybrid plasmode simulation built on mlmRev::egsingle. The simulation is implemented by RESI::hybridPlasmodeSim() (RESI/R/mixed_simulations.R) and run by tests/run_hybrid_plasmode.R.

Why not resample the real outcomes? An earlier full two-stage bootstrap of the real data (schools, then children, with replacement, keeping the observed outcomes) gave model-based fixed-effect SEs that stayed well below the Monte Carlo SD for child- and occasion-level covariates, and a growing bias in the school variance. Simon’s hypothesis is that real slope heterogeneity across schools and children, which Model A does not include, inflates the true sampling variability when real outcomes are resampled. Consistent with this, outcomes generated from the fitted Model A were correctly calibrated. The hybrid plasmode therefore resamples the covariate design hierarchically but generates new outcomes from the fitted model.

2 Dataset: mlmRev::egsingle

egsingle is a 3-level growth-curve dataset (measurement occasion nested in child nested in school) used as the plasmode base because it is the only dataset found (across lme4, nlme, geepack, mlmRev, JM, joineR, merTools) with >=1000 independent subjects, a continuous repeated-measures outcome, and a continuous time covariate suitable for a smooth term.

2.1 Overall size

Overall dataset size
Quantity N
Schools 60
Children 1721
Measurement occasions (rows) 7230

2.2 Children per school

Distribution of children per school (60 schools)
Min 1st Qu. Median Mean 3rd Qu. Max SD
5 15.75 24 28.68 40.25 89 18.13

Every one of the 60 schools has at least 5 children, up to 89, with a mean of 28.7 and median of 24 children per school (SD 18.1) – a right-skewed, moderately variable cluster-size distribution, which is why the plasmode resampling below draws each school’s own number of children (not a fixed number) when it is resampled.

2.3 Variables

egsingle variables and nesting structure
Variable Level Type Description
schoolid 3 (school, n=60) factor school identifier
childid 2 (child, n=1721) factor child identifier, nested in school
year 1 (occasion, n=7230 rows) continuous time, centered (range -2.5 to 2.5, integer steps)
grade 1 (occasion) continuous (0-4) grade level, collinear with year
math 1 (occasion) continuous outcome: math achievement score
retained 1 (occasion) binary factor held back a grade (mostly time-invariant)
female 2 (child) binary factor child sex
black 2 (child) binary factor child race indicator
hispanic 2 (child) binary factor child ethnicity indicator
size 3 (school) continuous school enrollment size
lowinc 3 (school) continuous % low income at school
mobility 3 (school) continuous % student mobility at school

3 Simulation design

3.1 Fixed-divisor covariate rescaling

size (school enrollment, range 113-1486, SD 312.6) is on a very different scale from the other covariates and caused an lme4 convergence warning when used raw. Both size and lowinc are rescaled by a fixed divisor (not a z-score), applied identically to every replicate, so coefficients stay directly interpretable:

  • size_100 = size / 100 (school enrollment in hundreds of students)
  • lowinc_10 = lowinc / 10 (percent low-income in units of 10 percentage points)

Combined with lmerControl(optimizer = "bobyqa", optCtrl = list(maxfun = 2e5)), Model A fits with 0 convergence warnings on the full data.

3.2 Model A

math ~ year + female + black + hispanic + size_100 + lowinc_10 + (1 | schoolid/childid)

The full-sample Model A fit uses ML (REML = FALSE) and supplies the plug-in generating parameters and full-sample reference. Each simulated Model A fit uses REML (REML = TRUE). Thus the replicate estimator is REML while the full-sample target/generating fit is ML; interpret finite-sample differences with that distinction in mind.

Random-effect (variance component) standard errors are not computed; only fixed-effect model-based SEs are compared against the Monte Carlo SD of each fixed effect across replicates. Variance-component point estimates are still tracked for bias.

4 Hybrid plasmode (hierarchical covariate and BLUP resampling)

4.1 Motivation and method

This hybrid plasmode resamples the covariate design hierarchically from the real data, then generates fresh random effects and residuals from the fitted Model A generator. This retains the empirical joint covariate distribution across schools and students without carrying over the real outcomes.

For each replicate, draw n_schools source schools with replacement from the 60 observed schools. Within each selected source school, draw students with replacement. If source school \(i\) contains \(m_i\) observed students, draw approximately \(n_{per\_site} m_i / \bar m\) students, where \(\bar m\) is the average observed school size. Thus expected sample size is proportional to source-school size and the average number drawn per generated school is approximately n_per_site; rounding makes the realized total vary slightly. Each selected student contributes all of their observed measurement rows. Every school and student draw receives a new ID, even when the same source school or student is selected more than once. This sampling is with replacement and occurs anew for every replicate.

Raw BLUPs are shrunk toward zero relative to the true random-effect variance (a well-known property of best linear unbiased prediction), so each BLUP pool is first centered to exactly mean zero and then rescaled so its variance equals the corresponding fitted variance component before any resampling: \[b^*_i = (b_i - \bar b) \times \sqrt{\hat\sigma^2 \Big/ \tfrac{1}{G}\textstyle\sum_i (b_i - \bar b)^2}\] The \(1/G\) (population) variance is used because generated units draw with replacement from the pool, so the variance of a draw is exactly \(\hat\sigma^2\). (An earlier version used the \(1/(G-1)\) sample variance, which built a \((G-1)/G\) shrinkage, \(-1.67\%\) for the 60 school BLUPs, into var_schoolid.) For Model A fit to the real data: the 60 school BLUPs have raw variance 0.056 (fitted var_schoolid = 0.079, so rescale factor \(\approx 1.19\)); the 1721 child BLUPs have raw variance 0.562 (fitted var_childid:schoolid = 0.652, rescale factor \(\approx 1.08\)). The full-data Model A fit remains ML (REML = FALSE) and supplies the plug-in DGP fixed effects and variance components. School and student BLUP pools are centered and rescaled to their fitted variances; each generated school and student receives an independent draw with replacement from its corresponding pool. Fresh residuals are drawn from the fitted Normal residual distribution. Each simulated dataset is refit using REML (REML = TRUE); the coefficient and RESI standard errors are model-based, from stats::vcov.

The reported grid is n_schools in {15,30,60,100} crossed with n_per_site in {25,100,200}. The 200-school and 50-student/site conditions are excluded. The simulation sets set.seed(2026) once before iterating over grid cells. mclapply uses L’Ecuyer-CMRG worker streams with mc.set.seed = TRUE for covariate resampling, BLUP resampling, and residual draws.

4.2 Results

Blank entries in the wide tables indicate conditions that were not simulated. The RESI table reports the mean and SD of the realized student count across replicates (n and n_sd), since proportional cluster-size sampling does not yield exactly n_schools * n_per_site students in every replicate. For the third plot row, the intercept and school-level predictors use n_schools; student-level and time-varying predictors use the planned student count n_schools * n_per_site. The realized student count and its SD are reported separately. This follows the between-school versus within-school scaling principle of Lyu and Welsh, treating repeated observations per student as bounded for this comparison. The reference is the Lyu and Welsh (2022) \(g, m \to \infty\) per-unit SE, \(\sqrt{n_k \mathrm{Var}(\hat\beta_k)}\), evaluated at the full-data ML parameter estimates (truth_se_scaled; see the RESI section for the formulas). It is fixed across designs. Each cell’s Monte Carlo SD of coefficient error is scaled by the square root of its planned count (n_schools for school-level terms; n_schools * n_per_site for student/time terms), then divided by that reference. The ratio should approach 1 as both n_schools and n_per_site grow. At finite n_per_site, school-level terms sit above 1, since their per-school variance is \(\tau^2_{school} + \sigma^2_w/m\) rather than \(\tau^2_{school}\). Partly clustered student terms (black, hispanic) sit slightly below 1, because they still borrow between-school information. The earlier full-sample ML SE reference corresponded to the observed \(m \approx 29\) and therefore drifted with n_per_site. Dashed curves show these ratios; the solid horizontal reference is 1.

The short translucent ticks in that row are the finite-sample reference for each cell. Each replicate redraws n_schools school profiles, so the Monte Carlo variance of \(\hat\beta\) is \(E_X[\mathrm{Var}(\hat\beta \mid X)] + \mathrm{Var}_X(E[\hat\beta \mid X])\), and the second term is about zero because \(\hat\beta\) is conditionally unbiased. The reference is therefore \(\sqrt{n_k E_X[V(X)]_{kk}}\), where \(V(X)\) is the GLS covariance of a resampled design at the full-data variance components, averaged over 2000 resampled school sets per cell (designAveragedSe() in RESI/R/mixed_simulations.R; cached in design_averaged_se.rds). It exceeds the SE of the expected design, \(\sqrt{n_k [E_X I(X)]^{-1}_{kk}}\), because \(E[I^{-1}] \ge E[I]^{-1}\). The gap is largest at small n_schools and for covariates concentrated in a few schools (e.g. hispanic: 28 of 60 schools have no Hispanic students), and it vanishes as n_schools grows. This reference applies to the spread of \(\hat\beta\) only. RESI divides by each dataset’s own SE, so its fixed-\(m\) reference in the RESI rows remains the expected-design value \(S_m\).

Joint hybrid plasmode calibration across n_schools and n_per_site. Left column: between-school terms (intercept, size_100, lowinc_10, school variance); middle column: terms that vary within school (year, female, black, hispanic, child and residual variances). The x-axis is the planned total student count n_schools x n_per_site (log scale). Solid lines connect n_per_site values at fixed n_schools; dotted lines connect n_schools values at fixed n_per_site; point shape marks n_schools; color marks the term and is shared across rows. Rows: fixed-effect SE ratio, variance-component relative bias, scaled Monte Carlo coefficient-error SD / Lyu-Welsh limiting per-unit SE (solid line at 1 = large-m truth; short translucent ticks = the design-averaged per-unit SE at that n_schools x n_per_site cell divided by the limiting SE, the finite-sample reference for the Monte Carlo SD), and RESI coefficient and ANOVA-term point estimates. In the RESI rows every quantity is centred on the large-m truth (Lyu-Welsh limit from the full-data ML fit, dashed zero line): points are simulation means and the wide translucent bands are the fixed-m truth S_m (exact RESI of the expected design at that n_per_site, constant across n_schools). Coefficients are multiplied by sign(S) so that positive means larger in magnitude in both RESI rows. The gap between points and the zero line is the total bias against the large-m target; the gap between points and the band is estimator bias at fixed m.

4.3 RESI point-estimator calibration

RESI is design dependent: for a fixed average cluster size \(m\), its value changes with \(m\) because the precision of between-school coefficients scales like \(g/(\tau^2_{school} + \sigma^2_{w}/m)\), and partly clustered student covariates (e.g. black, hispanic) borrow between-school information that vanishes as \(m\) grows. The calibration target, truth_resi, is therefore the Lyu and Welsh (2022, Theorem 1) increasing-cluster-size limit (\(g, m \to \infty\)), computed from the full-sample Model A ML fit by lyuLimitResi() (RESI/R/mixed_simulations.R):

  • between-school terms (intercept, size_100, lowinc_10), normalised by \(g\): \(S_k = \beta_k / \sqrt{\tau^2_{school}[C^{-1}]_{kk}}\), with \(C = g^{-1}\sum_s x_s x_s^\top\) over the 60 observed school profiles;
  • within-school terms, normalised by the student count \(N\) (level = 2): \(S_k = \beta_k / \sqrt{[(I_w/N)^{-1}]_{kk}}\), where \(I_w\) is the GLS information with the school intercept projected out (child random effect and residual retained);
  • ANOVA terms: \(S_T = \sqrt{\beta_T^\top (n_T V_{TT})^{-1} \beta_T}\) with no \(-\mathrm{df}\) correction.

expected_resi_m is the exact RESI under the expected resampled design at the given n_per_site (same formula, finite \(m\)); it equals the resi_pe full-data value at the observed mean school size and converges to truth_resi as \(m \to \infty\). truth_resi_full_data is the earlier resi_pe(truth_fit) reference (observed design, \(m \approx 29\), with the ANOVA \(-\mathrm{df}\) correction). The summary table reports bias as truth_resi - mc_mean_resi; the figure instead plots the simulation mean and expected_resi_m relative to truth_resi. Simulated datasets are refit by REML with model-based stats::vcov, and the fitted student count n is recorded for each design. These metrics calibrate the RESI point estimator only, not its sampling variance or confidence intervals.

4.4 Model B: child-level random slope for year

Model B adds a student-level random slope for year, math ~ year + female + black + hispanic + size_100 + lowinc_10 + (1 | schoolid) + (year | childid:schoolid) (tests/egsingle_models.R), and is run through the same 4 × 3 hybrid plasmode (Rscript tests/run_hybrid_plasmode.R B, seed 2026, 1000 replicates per cell). The simulation code handles general child-level random-effect designs \(Z_j\): the BLUPs are whitened and rescaled to the fitted child covariance \(G\), and the Lyu-Welsh within-school limit uses \(V_j = Z_j G Z_j^\top + \sigma^2 I\) in place of the random-intercept \(V_j\). The school level remains a random intercept. Because the random slope is at the child level, resi_pe keeps \(n = N\) students for year (a random slope at a coarser level, e.g. school, would make year’s \(n\) the number of schools).

Model B calibrates like Model A. The model-based SE ratios are within 0.92-1.05, all variance components (including the slope variance and the intercept-slope covariance) have relative bias below 1%, and the year RESI matches its Lyu limit at every design. The between-school terms show the same finite-\(m\) approach to the large-\(m\) limit as in Model A, tracked by the fixed-\(m\) truth \(S_m\).

4.5 Confidence interval coverage

tests/run_mixed_ci_coverage.R reruns the hybrid plasmode on n_schools \(\in \{15, 100\}\) × n_per_site \(\in \{25, 200\}\) (1000 replicates each). For each replicate it computes the RESI intervals of RESI:::.resi_ci_mixed() (derivation: notes/resi_mixed_ci.qmd) with:

  • the model-based covariance (stats::vcov, with the variance-component term), and
  • the school-clustered CR2 covariance;

each with the normal, QF and CF methods (coefficients are signed, so QF equals normal there). Coverage is scored against the fixed-\(m\) target \(S_m\) (expectedDesignResi) and the large-\(m\) Lyu limit \(S_{\text{Lyu}}\). The grey band is \(0.95 \pm 1.96\) Monte Carlo SE.

4.5.3 Finite-df reference for CR2 (package default)

The CR2 rows above use normal / \(\chi^2\) references. Because the CR2 meat is estimated from only \(g\) clusters, the package now uses a \(t_{g-1}\) / \(F(\cdot, g-1)\) reference automatically for cluster-robust intervals. Model-based intervals are unchanged (see notes/resi_mixed_ci.qmd, “Finite-df reference”). tests/run_cr2_reference_eval.R compares the two references at n_schools = 15 (1000 replicates per cell) on egsingle and on mlmRev::star (fresh seeds). The evaluation used a 200-point midpoint rule over \(W\). The package uses 20-node Gauss–Laguerre, which differs by at most \(3 \times 10^{-4}\) in tail probability.

4.5.4 nlme::lme fits

Each replicate is also refitted with nlme::lme(fixed, random = ~ 1 | schoolid/childid, method = "REML") (the replicate lmer fits are also REML) and passed through resi()’s lme path, which maps the fit to the same \(V = \sigma^2(I + Z\Lambda\Lambda^\top Z^\top)\) representation as lmer (see notes/resi_mixed_ci.qmd). The two engines optimise the same likelihood with different optimisers, so the intervals should agree up to the optimiser tolerance, and so should the coverage.

Results:

  • nlme’s default optimiser (nlminb) failed to converge in some replicates: 0, 69, 80 and 191 of 1000 in the four cells (g = 15, m = 25; 100, 25; 15, 200; 100, 200). lmer converged in all 1000. These are fitting failures in nlme::lme, not in the RESI code, but the lme coverage below is computed on the remaining replicates.
  • Where both engines fit, estimates agree to \(3 \times 10^{-4}\) and interval endpoints to \(5 \times 10^{-5}\)–\(4 \times 10^{-4}\), except the model-based intervals at g = 15, m = 25. There the largest endpoint difference is about 0.23, which is consistent with near-singular fits (\(\hat\tau^2_{\text{school}} \approx 0\)): lmer reaches the boundary, but lme’s log-scale parameterisation cannot, so the numerical Hessian of the \(\psi\) term differs. The effect on coverage there is at most 0.001.
  • Coverage differs from lmer by at most 0.012 in every cell.
  • The lmer rows reproduce the previous lmer-only run exactly (same seed).

4.6 Interpretation

  • Fixed-effect SE calibration and variance-component bias are shown across the joint n_schools by n_per_site grid in a single panel per diagnostic, plotted against the planned total student count.
  • The RESI rows separate the two sources of discrepancy from the large-\(m\) target. The band (\(S_m\) minus the Lyu limit) is the finite-\(m\) estimand gap. It is large for between-school terms, small for partly clustered student covariates (black, hispanic), and essentially zero for year and female, and it shrinks as n_per_site grows. The distance from the points to the band is estimator bias at fixed \(m\). It is negligible for coefficients. For ANOVA terms it is about \(1/(2 S n)\), from the \(-\mathrm{df}\) correction, truncation and square root, so it shrinks with n_schools for between-school terms. This approximation needs \(S\sqrt{n}\) to be large; for near-null terms (female, and size_100 at small n_schools) truncation at zero dominates instead. These are point-estimator diagnostics; interval coverage is in the next bullet.
  • CI coverage. With the model-based covariance, coverage of \(S_m\) is close to 0.95 in every cell (cell means 0.94-0.96; the lowest values, about 0.90-0.92, are for black/hispanic and lowinc_10 at n_schools = 15). The normal ANOVA interval undercovers the near-boundary terms at n_schools = 15; QF and CF do not. With CR2, coverage is 0.82-0.94 at n_schools = 15, because the estimated SD of the RESI underestimates its Monte Carlo SD by 20-30% there (the usual few-cluster behaviour), and 0.93-0.95 at n_schools = 100. The CR2 RESI is much more variable than the model-based one for terms with a large RESI and a small SE (e.g. year: Monte Carlo SD 0.29 vs 0.03 at n_schools = 100, n_per_site = 200). The school-level meat is estimated from only n_schools clusters, and the intervals reflect that variability. The package default for CR2 uses a \(t_{g-1}\) reference, which raises coverage by about 0.03 at 15 schools and 0.01 at 30; across the full grid, CR2-t coverage rises steadily towards 0.95 as n_schools grows. Model B (random slope) behaves like Model A with the model-based covariance. Its CR2 intervals undercover more at 15 schools. Coverage of \(S_{\text{Lyu}}\) matches coverage of \(S_m\) for within-school terms. For between-school terms it drops where the fixed-\(m\) gap is large relative to the interval width (lowinc_10: about 0.6 at n_schools = 100, n_per_site = 25), which is a property of the estimand, not of the interval.

5 Open questions / next steps

  • Simon’s slope-heterogeneity hypothesis (see Purpose) has not been confirmed directly for every term affected under full resampling of the real data. Model A contains no random slopes. Model B adds a child-level slope for year only; slopes for other terms, or school-level slopes, are not simulated.
  • For 100 schools, source-school covariate profiles are sampled repeatedly from the observed 60-school empirical distribution. Assessing sensitivity to this finite school-profile pool remains an interpretation caveat.
